title: The Field Worker Crowned at Gulbarga

title_i18n.en: The Field Worker Crowned at Gulbarga

subtitle: From Hasan Gangu to Alauddin Bahman Shah, a Deccan Crown is Forged
era: Founding of the Bahmani Sultanate, 1347-1358 CE
moral: New power must be judged by truth, not by legend.

sources.note: Near-contemporary Delhi account for Hasan Gangu's low origins and Tughluq service.

sources.citation: Muhammad Qasim Ferishta, Tarikh-i-Firishta / Gulshan-i-Ibrahimi, completed c. 1606
sources.note: Detailed later Deccan narrative for the 1347 founding, used with caution for legends.

sources.citation: Bahmani copper coins of the Gulbarga mint, 1347-1358, British Museum and related catalogues
sources.note: Physical evidence for independent Bahmani sovereignty and the first capital.

sources.citation: Richard M. Eaton, A Social History of the Deccan 1300-1761, Cambridge UP, 2005
sources.note: Modern critique of the Hasan Gangu origin stories and the Tughluq-crisis context.

panels.shot: sweeping low-angle wide of Alauddin Bahman Shah standing before Gulbarga fort, stormy Deccan sky behind

dialogue.text: In the troubled Deccan of 1347, a field commander named Hasan Gangu cast off Delhi’s shadow and rose as Alauddin Bahman Shah, founding a kingdom whose truth lies deeper than its legends.

panels.shot: bird's-eye view of the Deccan plateau with routes from Delhi snaking south

dialogue.text: By the 1340s, the Delhi Sultanate’s reach had pushed deep into the Deccan, but its grip was weakening. Costly campaigns, harsh experiments, and distance frayed the bonds between Delhi and its southern soldiers.

panels.shot: wide shot of Daulatabad fort looming over rocky hills at dusk

dialogue.text: At Daulatabad, the Tughluq experiment of ruling the Deccan from a second capital had left wounds. Barani notes officers unpaid, garrisons restless, and commanders who measured loyalty against survival.

panels.shot: medium shot of young Hasan Gangu among rank-and-file soldiers in a dusty camp

dialogue.text: Barani calls him a man of humble origin, a field worker raised into the army. In the Deccan camps, Hasan Gangu learned dust, discipline, and the hard lessons of serving a far-off court.

panels.shot: close-up on Hasan’s face lit by campfire, half in shadow

dialogue.speaker: alauddin_bahman_shah
dialogue.text: If they command without justice, how long must we obey?

panels.shot: dynamic wide of a rebel assembly of Deccani amirs in a rugged landscape

dialogue.text: In this unsettled world, Deccani amirs began to defy Delhi. Eaton notes how the south’s military elites, mostly long-serving officers, turned rebellion into a bid for their own sovereignty.

panels.shot: mid-wide of Hasan Gangu speaking to a small cluster of officers in a fortified courtyard

dialogue.text: Hasan rose among them as a capable commander, trusted in battle and negotiation. Barani records his service under the Tughluqs, yet it is in this moment that he begins to become more than a servant.

panels.shot: interior wide of a simple hall where a local leader Ismail Mukh is being acclaimed on a makeshift throne

dialogue.text: When the Tughluq hold cracked, the Deccani nobles first set up Ismail Mukh as their leader. Ferishta names him, a figurehead for revolt, while Delhi’s writ shrank to roads and garrisons.

panels.shot: medium shot of Hasan Gangu standing respectfully before Ismail Mukh in the same hall

dialogue.text: Yet power on the ground rested with Hasan and the rebel commanders. Ferishta describes councils where they quietly measured Ismail’s symbolic rule against Hasan’s command of men and fortresses.

panels.shot: intimate medium of Ismail placing his hand on Hasan’s shoulder in a dim audience chamber

dialogue.text: According to Ferishta, the choice was stark: a fragile symbol or a tested general. Ismail is said to have abdicated, asking Hasan to lead, so that the new Deccan state might survive the storms to come.

panels.shot: epic wide of the coronation ground near Gulbarga with gathered amirs and soldiers

dialogue.text: On 3 August 1347, near Gulbarga, the field commander stepped forward to become a king. The day marked not just a ceremony, but the birth of a Deccan sultanate independent of Delhi.

panels.shot: low-angle close-medium of Hasan as he receives the ceremonial turban and takes a new name

dialogue.text: Hasan Gangu took the throne-name Alauddin Bahman Shah. The title echoed older Persian lineages, a deliberate claim that this new kingdom would stand among the great houses of Islam.

panels.shot: tight close-up on Alauddin Bahman Shah’s hand grasping the hilt of a sheathed sword

dialogue.speaker: alauddin_bahman_shah
dialogue.text: From today, this land shall not be a province, but a kingdom.

panels.shot: wide of Gulbarga’s walls and emerging cityscape under construction

dialogue.text: Alauddin Bahman Shah chose Gulbarga as his capital. The city’s walls, palaces, and congregational mosque began to grow, staking the Bahmani claim in stone across the Deccan.

panels.shot: macro close-up of an early Bahmani copper coin on a craftsman’s palm

dialogue.text: Copper coins from Gulbarga bear his name and titles, the metal testimony of sovereignty. Where myths spin stories, these coins silently confirm a new state issuing its own authority.

panels.shot: interior wide of Alauddin on a simple throne hearing petitions from Deccani soldiers and settlers

dialogue.text: Eaton describes how the Deccan’s society began to reshape around this court. Old soldiers, traders, and scholars sought favor and order from a sultan who had once shared their hardships.

panels.shot: moody wide of a distant battlefield between Bahmani and southern forces, seen from afar

dialogue.text: In later decades, Bahmani rulers would fight Vijayanagara and others in brutal campaigns. Ferishta writes of devastating warfare in the Carnatic, and of captured soldiers sometimes converted and drawn into new armies.

panels.shot: evening medium of an older Alauddin Bahman Shah on the ramparts of Gulbarga, looking out

dialogue.text: Alauddin ruled until 1358, laying the frame of a kingdom others would expand, fracture, and fight over. Barani’s field worker had become the founding sultan of a line that reshaped the Deccan.

panels.shot: slow push-in close-up on Alauddin’s contemplative face, half-lit by lamplight

dialogue.text: Legends later wrapped him in noble ancestry and miracle tales, yet coins, chronicles, and the stone of Gulbarga still recall a harsher truth: a field worker who seized a crown, and a kingdom born from fracture.
